en: He cut fat from the choicest meat and fed you;
So that you might become a special kinsman,
His mother Kanykey let you suck
At both her pure breasts.
When you sucked Kanykey’s left breast,
Black blood came forth.
“This suckling will become an enemy,”
His mother Kanykey cried in anguish.
“He will never be kin—let him go!
At heart he is an enemy by birth;
Slaughter this wretch!” she said.
But the panther was magnanimous,
He would not heed malicious words
And disobeyed his mother Kanykey.
Though your tongue sounds gentle,
You will never mend, Kanchoro;
At heart you are an enemy to the end.
Understand the wisdom of my words;
My precious one, my friend,
Heed what I say.
Why should we provoke the blessed gray-maned hero
And bring harm upon ourselves?
Lay down your anger, Kanchoro;
Come, let us depart safely to the borderlands.
Can a full-grown warrior
Prosper after defiling another’s salt?
Can there ever be another
Who wrecks a nation and corrupts its people?
Understand the wisdom of my words;
Do not leave your people destitute—
My noble friend, heed what I say!
From this hero Semetey
The lands of Jylgyn and Keng-Kol will remain,
And from him the white-capped Kyrgyz nation will remain;
The wretched will join these deeds into songs,
And if tomorrow the new generation
Should seek rest, it will stir up strife.
They will bind their pinewood spears
And wage war with hatred fixed in their hearts.
Think on this, Kanchoro:
To our right are the Russians,
On your flank are the Chinese,
Before you stand the riflemen;
Many enemies are waiting
To contend with us.
Why should we fight to the bitter end
Against this deeply rooted gray wolf?
Come, let us leave, Jediger.
If word that the Kyrgyz are slaughtering one another
Should reach the Chinese,
If their moon-crested banners fill the land,
If a clamor rends the sky,
If dust flies into the heavens
As their army comes swarming,
Who will wield the blood-dark, keen-edged sword
Without letting it waver?
Who will lead this great Kyrgyz nation,
Keeping the infidel’s wrath at bay
And sparing the people grief?
That gray wolf Semetey is not dead;
That noble man has not entered
The true abode from which none return.
When the bloodthirsty foe thrust his spear,
I believe Semetey was merely wounded;
Vanishing beyond the eye’s sight,
I believe he passed into the unseen world.
If death has not yet reached him,
If by chance he remains alive,
May the great host of the Kara-Jediger
Not meet utter destruction together;
May he not slaughter us all.
May he not mount his dapple-gray horse in fury,
Nor suddenly turn back
And punish the rebels without mercy;
May he not charge with a shout and lowered spear
And pitilessly slaughter the people.
Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
May the offspring of that enraged lion
Not come down upon our necks;
May he not scatter our four kinds of livestock.
If by chance he grows furious,
If rage should darken his face,
May he not break our ranks.
Great host of the Kara-Jediger,
Let us not assail the wrathful lion,
Become needlessly entangled in disaster,
Be caught in a raging flood,
And have so many of us slaughtered;
Let us not perish in a massacre,
Nor let so many of us become a spectacle;
Let us not die under oppression.
When I consider all that has passed and all to come,
Kanchoro, son of Chubak,
My friend, when I weigh your every intention,
There is something strange in your words,
And something singularly quarrelsome in you.
Your words are evasive;
When I measure and watch your conduct,
I find the quarrel lies within you.
This brave Semey, son of the bloodthirsty hero—
And you, Kanchoro, son of Chubak—
When you were orphaned of your father,
He cherished you more than his own kin.
Kanykey gave you her left breast,
You infidel slave, and nursed you;
Semetey was magnanimous
And regarded you as his own nestmate.
Keeping you beside him, he made you a warrior,
Making you the equal of grown champions,
A lion capable of shaking the world;
He raised your little soul to greatness,
And set your wretched life aright.
He clothed you in armor no bullet could pierce,
Mounted you on a steed no bullet could catch,
And sent you shouting against the foe.
He carved meat for you and fed you,
And made not only the Kyrgyz, but all mankind,
Call you Kanchoro the hero.
He equipped you and sent you forth with your spear,
And spread your fame among the people.
He built you a stately walled dwelling,
And every enemy who challenged you
He fought and laid to rest.
Over the Argyn and the Kyrgyz
He made you governor, sultan, and khan.
Now Semetey proved a mighty lion,
Yet when you grew fat, without so much
As a coal-black fault from him, your heart turned corrupt—
You, Kanchoro, son of Chubak.
How did you grow so powerful?
You defiled your oath and threw the people into turmoil;
You plotted evil against your elder brother.
Chynkojo and you are alike—
You have proved a worthless companion.
May there never be another like you,
A companion who is no true hero.
You turn all before you into prey,
Yet call yourself a heroic companion.
Filled utterly with treachery,
You are an infidel companion.
You covet whatever pleases you
And seize it for yourself.
If that famous rumor is truly true,
To the very depths of hell
You are destined to go.
In the end, consumed by flames,
You are destined to remain there.
Into every calamity and affliction
You are destined to go.
Whoever heeds your words,
Into the torment of true hell
You are destined to cast.
Into the great strife that destroys nations
You are destined to go.
You regard your own kinsman
As though he were an enemy.
Destroying nations and corrupting peoples,
You are a companion who betrays them.
To every grave affliction
You are all too ready to yield.
Those who call you friend
You hand over to punishment
With your own hands, my friend.
In your own mind you strut proudly,
Thinking yourself a mighty friend.
Treacherous in thought and forked of tongue,
You have proved a corrupt friend.
Let me tell of your corruption:
You became the enemy of your own elder brother.
Can one such as you be a hero?
What good is it to call you one?
You are calamity that never passes,
The very black eye of disaster.
You were born, poor wretch,
The very embodiment of one who ruins nations.
You are the black eye of conflict—
Not merely its eye, but conflict itself.
Semetey is the halter of the nation,
His fame known to all the people.
The quarrel that shook nations and ruined peoples
Was caused by that slave Chynkojo.
Had Chynkojo not existed,
The wise and valiant Toltoy,
Would not, because of Chynkojo,
Have stood on opposing sides,
Tearing lungs and kindling fury,
Fighting one another in resentment.
There was no white-ridged mountain between them,
Nor were they enemies destined to slaughter each other.
It was the cruelty of that slave Chynkojo—
And now, Kanchoro, it is your tyranny.
Understand what I have told you;
Oh, dearest friend, heed my words!
Let us not turn aside into rebellion,
Nor raise a hand against this bloodthirsty hero
Whom Khizir has blessed.
Why assail the lionhearted hero
And needlessly become entangled in suffering?
Why remain stubborn?
Come, dearest friend, let us leave.
Let us have no part in quarrel or conflict.
This Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Is a warrior equal to us both;
Let us not attack the poor man.
He is a blazing red ember,
Unmatched among all creation;
He is a steel bullet against the foe,
A fiery champion beyond all others.
His right shoulder is broad,
And all twelve parts of his body are perfectly formed.
When an enemy presses hard upon the Kyrgyz,
He is the lion whose mere presence confronts them.
This formidable hero Külchoro
Is the warrior who receives their assault,
A fortress established for the Kyrgyz,
A defensive stronghold of iron.
Pure in thought and generous in spirit,
He is a lion who spares no effort.
Not only the Kyrgyz, but all mankind
He is one capable of defending.
Let us have no part in musket-fire or conflict;
Heed my words, dearest friend—
Let us leave without attacking Külchoro!
He is the very embodiment of a gray-wolf hero;
Why persist in defying him?
Come, dearest friend, let us leave!
Let us tell the people
That Külchoro is such a man.
Without rebellion or warfare,
Come, dearest friend, let us turn back.
Why contend in anger
With this gray wolf blessed by Khizir?
Lest there be a massacre,
Come, my friend, let us leave!
I have seen Külchoro’s form:
Tall in stature and broad of shoulder,
Both a wrestler and a lionhearted warrior—
No hero like him can be found
Anywhere in the world.
He is blue-gray as tempered steel,
Steadfast in a true massacre.
Let us not stumble into disaster
Or involve ourselves in a terrible conflict.
Let us lead the finest steeds unsaddled
And load them with yellow gold.
Let us present every swift charger
As a gift to Külchoro.
Heed me, my friend; let us turn back!
Let us consent to what he asks;
To the young champion, Almambet’s son,
Let us give whatever he desires.
Gold coins, gold, and these matchless steeds—
Let us hold none back, but offer them all.
Without grappling or fighting,
For mercy’s sake, my friend, let us turn back!
Let us become as a wind from the qibla,
